title: Advent with Isaiah
hook: Advent's first readings come mostly from Isaiah: a people that walked in darkness

segments.voice: Yesterday, the First Sunday of Advent: a house at night and a porter told to stay awake. Your line was one word, watch. What did you catch, being awake? Day six hundred thirty-four.

Sit in the pew on a weekday in early Advent and listen to the first reading. Day after day, the reader opens with the same words: a reading from the book of the prophet Isaiah. Swords beaten into plowshares. A wolf lying down with a lamb. A shoot from a stump. The desert blooming. Isaiah is the voice the Church hands Advent, so much that some people call him the Advent prophet. And the Isaiah line the Church saves for Christmas night is about people in the dark.
screen: `A READING FROM ISAIAH.` → `PLOWSHARES, WOLF, SHOOT.` → `PEOPLE IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the days of King Ahaz and King Hezekiah. His world was frightening: Assyria, the great power of the day, was swallowing the small kingdoms around Judah, and Isaiah himself names the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up by the Sea of Galilee, as the ones brought low. Into that darkness Isaiah speaks a sentence in the past tense, as if the rescue had already happened. The Douay-Rheims reads: "The people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light." Light is risen, he says, on those in the region of the shadow of death. Then a child: a son is given, and the government will rest on his shoulder, and his names pile up, ending with Prince of Peace. Jewish readers place this in Isaiah's own time, and some Jewish commentators have understood the child as a king of Judah, Hezekiah. Christians read it as well as a promise fulfilled in Jesus, and Matthew's Gospel quotes the darkness-and-light line when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the very region Isaiah named. Both readings live with the same words. Why give Isaiah to Advent? Because Advent is about waiting in the dark without pretending it's already bright. Isaiah never says the darkness is small. He says a light shows up inside it. And Catholics hear this passage at the Mass during the night of Christmas, so Advent's prophet gets the first word of Christmas too. In early December the nights in the northern half of the world keep getting longer. The readings answer the calendar with one stubborn sentence.
screen: `ASSYRIA AND THE DARK NORTH.` · `A GREAT LIGHT, IN THE PAST TENSE.` · `A CHILD, A SON, A PRINCE OF PEACE.` · `SAVED FOR CHRISTMAS NIGHT.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Isaiah 9:2, slowly, once. If you have a Bible nearby, find it. If not, hold the line you just heard: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. Then sit. Bring to mind one dark place you know, in your own life or in the news, without fixing it. Just let the sentence sit beside it. If you pray, you can hold that place up in the light. If you don't, simply keep both in view. The bell holds the time.
Advent with Isaiah. The season's first readings come mostly from the prophet Isaiah, who promised light to people walking in darkness. Today's word.
Your line: a great light. Today, notice the first light you switch on after dark, and let it remind you of Isaiah's sentence. Day six hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Through Advent, the first reading at Mass is very often from Isaiah, and Isaiah 9 is read at the Mass during the night of Christmas.

fork.setup: you're Isaiah. Assyria has just swallowed the northern lands, and the people are terrified. how do you speak?
options: tell them the danger is smaller than it looks.
speak of the light as if it has already come.
tell them to flee south and say nothing more.
fork.reveal: he doesn't shrink the darkness. he says, in the past tense, that a great light has already risen inside it.

original.note: Hebrew: a great light, from Isaiah 9 (9:1 in Hebrew Bibles).

trapdoor: what you thought: Isaiah is a Christmas-card prophet.
what it means: a prophet in a frightening time who promised light to people walking in darkness, read all through Advent.
what a scholar hears: the oracle is in the prophetic past tense; some Jewish commentators have seen the child as Hezekiah, and Matthew 4 reads it of Jesus in Galilee.
